text:
The coefficient map is the derived law written as v = Σ n_m c^m / Σ d_m c^m, where c^m runs over concentration monomials (1, A, B, AB, PQ, …) and each coefficient n_m, d_m is an expression in the mechanism's constants. rate_law_coefficients(m) would return those two maps. Textbook kinetic constants are ratios of coefficients, for example Ka = d(B)/d(AB) and V1 = n(AB)/d(AB) for a bi-bi law, so kinetic_constants(m) returns V1, V2, Ka, Kia, … as expressions in your constants (or numbers given parameter values), and is_rate_law(m, f) checks a textbook formula exactly.

Tests written in microscopic constants (the Segel transcriptions in k1f, k1r, …) keep working: they are checked against the AllParameters law, and all 26 matched exactly in the probe. Only the glue that maps k1f, k1r, … to the package's names changes. Today it relies on the as-written step order (a DSL feature that exists only for tests, plus 184 lines of helpers); the proposal keys it by role instead (the forward constant of the step that binds A to E), about 25 lines.

The Cleland layer is an addition for stating textbook equations in V, Km and Ki; it replaces nothing.

Follow-up: these are two separate things.

- The coefficient map is package code: it reads a derived law's coefficients and can name Cleland ratios.
- The test bridge is test code: it tells a Segel transcription which package constant its k1f is. It never uses coefficients, so dropping Cleland leaves every test written in microscopic constants untouched.

Today's bridge, for Segel Ordered Bi Bi:

- A test-only macro returns the steps in written order, a DSL feature that exists only for these tests.
- By then the Step constructor has stored the written releases as bindings, so the order survives but the written direction does not.
- A helper numbers the stored steps by written position and puts each stored-forward constant on k{i}f.
- It then swaps f and r wherever the stored step binds a product, guessing that the textbook wrote that step as a release.

By role: the test reads the written steps from its own macro block, finds the stored step with the same two sides, and reads that step's constants in the written direction. k3f is k_EAB_to_EQ_P because the block says E(A, B) <--> E(Q) + P. There is no guess and nothing needs source order from the package, so the parser returns only the mechanism.

- I ran it. It gives the same k values as today's bridge on all 34 specs with an analytical oracle (26 plain, 8 allosteric), and all 34 oracles match rate_equation.
- It is 56 lines, not the 25 I estimated. With the parts that stay, the bridge shrinks from about 207 to about 110 lines.
- The five allosteric call sites that attach tags by position would write the tags inline instead (not yet tried).

Identifiability: Cleland constants give no advantage.

- The identifiable rank equals the rank of the coefficient map in 806 of 806 laws.
- Cleland constants are not a minimal set: ordered bi-bi has 7 fitted constants at rank 7 but 8 free Cleland constants, which obey a third, non-monomial relation.
- They fix none of the 5 rank-deficient enumerated laws, and they inflate rank-full ones (init_bibi/55 goes from 5 to 7).

Fitting in identifiable coordinates would make the fitted count equal the rank. But it needs a basis chosen per law, positivity constraints and new bounds: a separate, later idea.

So drop Cleland. I now recommend keeping the bridge in the tests, rewritten by role; the coefficient extraction that normalization needs stays internal.
